_comment: Skill_Catalog — which Agent Space receives which skill, and which agent
types each skill is offered to.
This file is the ONE place both of those decisions are declared. Both
scripts/package-skills.sh (which builds dist/skills/<space>/) and
scripts/upload-skills.sh (which uploads and prints the per-space plan) read
it, so adding a skill means adding one entry under .skills and one line
under a space's "skills" list, and nothing else.
Why a manifest and not a frontmatter field in each SKILL.md: the routing
decision is about deployment topology (which space owns which runbook), not
about the runbook's content, and it has to be reviewable in both directions
at once — 'what does the platform space get' is a question about the set, not
about any single skill. A SKILL.md also has to stay portable: the same file
is loaded by the custom Strands agents from the container image, where
'agent space' means nothing.
Both scripts fail loudly on a mismatch in EITHER direction: a skill listed
here with no agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, or a skill folder that no space
claims. A silently unpackaged skill is the failure this file exists to stop.
── .skills[<name>].agentTypes — WHEN the space may load the skill ─────────
metadata.agent_types is required by the DevOps Agent asset API for skill
assets, and it is a HARD GATE: a skill scoped to a phase the run never
enters is simply never eligible, with no error and no journal entry. That
already cost us a demo — all six skills were first uploaded as
["INCIDENT_TRIAGE"], so the four backend runbooks were invisible during
root-cause analysis, which is the only phase they were written for. The
ddb-throttle skills-ON run measured a space without its catalog.
The enum is not in the service model (metadata is a free-form Document).
The service enumerates it in the ValidationException for an unknown value:
GENERIC, CHAT, INCIDENT_TRIAGE, INCIDENT_RCA, INCIDENT_MITIGATION,
PREVENTION, CHANGE_REVIEW, CHANGE_RELEASE, QUALITY_ASSURANCE_TESTING,
RELEASE_SHEPHERD, RELEASE_READINESS_REVIEW, RELEASE_TESTING,
SYSTEM_LEARNING, INCIDENT_UI
The user guide's labels map onto the incident phases as Generic = GENERIC
(the default, applies to ALL agent types), On-demand = CHAT, Incident Triage
= INCIDENT_TRIAGE (decide WHETHER to investigate — the docs' own example is a
skill that SKIPS incidents), Incident RCA = INCIDENT_RCA, Incident
Mitigation = INCIDENT_MITIGATION, Evaluation = PREVENTION.
SECOND CONSTRAINT, also undocumented: GENERIC is exclusive. Sending
["INCIDENT_RCA", "GENERIC"] is rejected with 'GENERIC agent type cannot be
combined with other agent types'. So the choice per skill is binary — either
GENERIC alone (every phase) or an explicit phase list with no GENERIC in it.
There is no 'RCA plus a safety net' option.
Given that, every skill here is ["GENERIC"]. GENERIC is a superset of any
phase list, including INCIDENT_RCA, so it cannot be narrower than the intent;
and the failure we are recovering from is precisely a too-narrow scope
disabling a skill with no error and no journal entry. The cost of GENERIC is
a slightly larger candidate set the agent then filters by description — which
is why the descriptions carry the concrete alarms and services. The cost of
being too narrow is a skill that never loads at all. Until a journal shows a
phase-scoped skill actually loading, GENERIC is the only scope we can verify.
frontend-triage      ["GENERIC"] — it has to be live in BOTH phases: during
triage to decide local-vs-delegate, and during RCA to
actually make the delegation MCP call. Scoping it to
either phase alone breaks the other half, and GENERIC
is the only value that covers both.
report-standards     ["GENERIC"] — every run of every phase ends in a
report, including on-demand queries.
untrusted-content-   ["GENERIC"] — input-handling rules have to be in
handling             force before the first read and still in force at
the last write, so they span every phase. Scoping
them to one phase would leave the others reading
workload-authored text with no framing at all. Both
spaces get it: the app-team space ingests logs and
peer findings, the platform space ingests backend
telemetry and KB passages.
the four backend     ["GENERIC"] — these are root-cause procedures, so
runbooks             INCIDENT_RCA is the phase that describes them, and it
is confirmed accepted by the API. GENERIC is used
anyway because it is a superset of INCIDENT_RCA and the
exclusivity rule above forbids carrying both. Narrowing
to INCIDENT_RCA alone is the change to make only once a
journal has shown a phase-scoped skill loading.
The self-managed fallback agents are NOT covered by either field: they load
agents/skills/ from their container image, so they are unaffected by the
split and have no notion of agent types.

app-team.role: First responder in the frontend/app domain. Triages the user-visible symptom, resolves app-domain incidents locally, and delegates backend suspects to the platform space.

platform.role: Backend/platform investigator. Receives delegated tasks naming a backend suspect and runs the matching service-level runbook.
